title: Agent Front Door manifest
description: The document a caller receives when it opens a session with a party at that party's own domain. It answers one question: what does this endpoint expose, what can I do with each thing, where should I look for more, and what must I obey. It is a data document, not a web page: no layout, no script, no navigation, and no marketing beyond one line per agent. Every member is documented here so that an implementer can produce a valid document from this file alone; the numbered requirements in normative/MANIFEST.md state the obligations that go with each member. It is delivered as the first frame of a `portico/1` session and is never fetched from a URL.
$comment: additionalProperties is true by design: MAN-3 requires a client to ignore members it does not recognise, which is how this object grows without a flag day. A publisher MUST NOT rely on that to smuggle in a member a client is expected to act on.

agents.name: support
agents.description: Questions about service, coverage and pricing

manifest_version.description: The version of this document's shape, as MAJOR.MINOR. This is a compatibility promise to clients, and it is a different number from the specification's release tag: a release tag never moves, while this version grows when members are added. A client reads it to decide which members it may rely on. Absence is legal and means 1.0 (MAN-53); a present value that is not MAJOR.MINOR is invalid.

protocol.description: The wire protocol this endpoint speaks, as a token such as portico/1. It tells a caller what it may send after the document, and it lets a business advertise that it speaks something newer without changing this schema. Required.

endpoint.description: Identity of the service that answered: the place the caller connected to, which is distinct from any agent behind it. One business may run several endpoints.

agents.description: The things a caller can talk to here. Each entry is one addressable counterparty with its own description, and either holds a conversation or answers a single message. Required, and may be empty: an endpoint that answers but currently exposes nothing is a valid document, not an error, and a caller must read an empty list as 'this endpoint is up and offers nothing right now'.

examples.name: orders
examples.description: Take food orders: pizzas, sides, drinks

links.description: Documents this business publishes that a caller may want to read. Each carries a relation saying what it is, so a caller can tell a menu from an OpenAPI document from a status page. Replaces the deprecated 'refs' map, which could carry only a key and a URL.

capabilities.description: What this endpoint actually implements beyond the protocol minimum. A capability advertised here must be honoured: true means accepted, false or absent means rejected with a documented error. This is not the same as what the protocol permits.

limits.description: Operational limits a caller should expect to meet at endpoint level. A limit is a statement of intent, not a guarantee: a caller must still handle a rate_limited error. Absence means unknown, never unlimited.

session.description: Default session policy for agents at this endpoint. An agent may override it; the endpoint value is what applies when an agent does not.

generated_at.description: When this document was produced, as an RFC 3339 timestamp. Optional, and deliberately omitted by a daemon that delivers the manifest inside a handshake: the handshake itself is the freshness, because the document was read at the moment of use. A publisher that emits it must keep it stable for unchanged state, or the digest changes for no reason.

expires_at.description: When this document should be considered out of date, as an RFC 3339 timestamp. Optional, and only meaningful for a document published as a standalone file: a manifest delivered inside a session is fresh by construction, and a caller must not treat one received in a handshake as expired because of this member. A caller acting on a standalone document past this time must re-read it before relying on it.

digest.description: Integrity check over this document: 'sha256:' followed by 64 lowercase hex characters, computed as the SHA-256 of the RFC 8785 (JCS) canonical form of the document with 'digest' and 'signature' removed. It proves the bytes were not altered in transit or in a cache; it does not prove who wrote them, because anyone can compute one. A client must compute it over the bytes it received rather than over a re-encoded copy, or it will disagree with a correct publisher.

signature.description: Reserved for manifest signing, which is not designed yet. It must be present and null at manifest_version 1.1 and above; a client must ignore any object it does not understand rather than failing. Signing is an open question in the specification, and until it is settled a caller has integrity from the digest but not authenticity.

refs.description: Deprecated. A map of short key to URL, superseded by 'links' because a key cannot say what the target is. Still accepted and still emitted alongside 'links' for one release so that existing publishers keep working; a new implementation should emit 'links' and ignore this.

commands.description: Deprecated. The session operations this endpoint advertises, as a flat list of strings, superseded by 'capabilities.session' because a list cannot say what is actually accepted without contradiction. Still accepted and emitted for one release; a new implementation should read 'capabilities.session' and ignore this.

endpoint.title: endpoint
endpoint.description: The service that answered. This is the place, not an agent: a business with several offerings still has one endpoint per host and port, and each of its agents is listed separately.

id.description: A stable, opaque identifier for this endpoint that survives restarts and outlives a change of display name. A caller may keep bookkeeping against it. It is not an address and must not be used to reach the endpoint.

name.description: Display name for the endpoint, shown to a human. It is presentation only: a caller must not use it to address anything, and two different endpoints may share one.

description.description: One line of plain text saying what this business does. No markup is assumed renderable, and a caller must not present it as if the business had answered a question with it.

agent.title: agent
agent.description: One thing a caller can talk to at this endpoint. An agent is either conversational, meaning a session is required and several turns share context, or stateless, meaning each message stands alone. The distinction is the single most important member in this object: it decides whether a caller must open a session before it may send anything.

name.description: The address of this agent within the manifest, and the value a caller sends in the 'agent' field of a message. It must start with a letter or digit and may continue with letters, digits, dot, underscore or hyphen, up to 64 characters. It must be unique within the document. Treat it as an address, not a label: changing it breaks every caller that stored it, so a publisher should keep the old name alongside a new one for at least one release.

id.description: An optional stable identifier for the agent that survives a change of 'name'. A caller that keeps long-lived bookkeeping should prefer this for the record and 'name' for addressing. Unique within the document when present.

description.description: One sentence of plain text saying what this agent does, written as capability rather than marketing. A caller may show it verbatim when a model is choosing between agents, and must not pass it off as an answer from the business. Two agents whose descriptions are indistinguishable make the choice arbitrary, so a publisher should keep them distinct.
examples: Take food orders: pizzas, sides, drinks, pickup or delivery

tags.description: Free-form lowercase labels a program can filter on without asking a model to read prose. Advisory only: not a capability claim, not a whitelist, not a promise about behaviour. Unique within the agent. Keep them few and stable, because renaming one breaks a caller that filters on it.

sessions.description: Whether this agent holds a conversation. True means a caller must open a session and send its id with every turn, and turns accumulate into one exchange. False means the agent answers single messages and keeps nothing, and a caller must not send a session id at all. Required, because it decides how the agent is addressed: a client must read it before its first message.

start_message.description: A greeting the endpoint produces itself when a conversation with this agent is created. It is not a backend answer, it consumes no turn, and it is not a reply to anything. A caller may show it as the opening line of a conversation, which is why it can make an empty first message meaningful.
examples: Hello! Ask me anything about the restaurant.

links.description: Documents specific to this agent rather than to the whole endpoint, such as the menu an ordering agent works from.

limits.description: Limits that apply to this agent specifically, overriding the endpoint value for any member present. Absence means the endpoint limit applies.

session.description: Session policy for this agent, overriding the endpoint default for any member present. Only meaningful when 'sessions' is true.

refs.description: Deprecated per-agent equivalent of the top-level 'refs' map, superseded by this agent's 'links'. Accepted and emitted for one release for compatibility.

examples.name: orders
examples.description: Take food orders: pizzas, sides, drinks, pickup or delivery
examples.start_message: Hello! Ask me anything about the restaurant.

examples.name: status
examples.description: Opening hours and current waiting time

links.title: links
links.description: A list of published references. Each carries what it is as well as where it is, so a caller can decide whether to read it without fetching it.

link.title: link
link.description: One published reference: where it is and what it is.

rel.description: The relation type, a lowercase token naming what the target is, for example 'menu', 'docs', 'status' or 'openapi'. It starts with a letter and may continue with lowercase letters, digits, dot, underscore or hyphen. A client must not require any particular value, because a business chooses its own; an unknown relation means the target is simply not one the client knows how to use.

href.description: An absolute URI for the reference. It must carry a scheme: a relative path is not a published reference, because a caller has no document it is relative to.

label.description: A short human-readable name for the target, for display. Optional: when absent, a client may show the relation instead.

type.description: The media type of the target when known, such as text/html or application/pdf, so a caller can decide how to read it. Optional and advisory.

description.description: One line of plain text saying what the target contains. Optional.

capabilities.title: capabilities
capabilities.description: What this endpoint implements beyond the protocol minimum. The rule that makes this member trustworthy: anything advertised true must be accepted, and anything false or absent must be refused with a documented error rather than silently ignored. An endpoint that has not implemented the protocol at all advertises nothing here.

session.description: Which session operations this endpoint accepts. Each is a separate boolean rather than a list so that turning one off cannot silently turn another off, and so the member can grow without ambiguity. These are the authoritative statement of what a caller may do; the deprecated 'commands' list is not.

new.description: Whether a caller may create a session. Must be available for every agent that declares sessions: a conversational agent without session creation is unusable, so advertising false while listing such an agent is a contradiction, not a configuration.

get.description: Whether a caller may read a session envelope by id.

list.description: Whether a caller may browse its own sessions with this agent. Turning this off disables browsing only; creating, reading and closing must keep working.

close.description: Whether a caller may close a session, after which it can no longer be resumed.

prune.description: Whether a caller may ask the endpoint to delete expired and closed sessions past a retention period. Destructive, so a caller should not call it casually.

progress.description: Whether this endpoint reports progress inside a turn, so a caller can show that work is still happening before an answer arrives. A server must not send progress when this is absent or false.

cancel.description: Whether a caller may abandon a turn in flight. Cancellation is cooperative and best effort: it stops the wait and asks the backend to stop, and it does not roll back work the backend already committed.

max_turn_seconds.description: The longest a single turn is expected to take, in seconds, so a caller can set its own timeout sensibly instead of guessing. Advisory: a turn that exceeds it may still be legitimate, but a caller may reasonably give up.

limits.title: limits
limits.description: Advertised operational limits. A limit states intent so a caller can pace itself; it is not a guarantee, and a caller must still handle a rate_limited error. Absence of a member means that limit is unknown, which is never the same as unlimited.

max_message_bytes.description: The largest message, in bytes, the endpoint will accept. Bounded above by the protocol's 8 MiB frame cap, which is a property of the framing rather than a policy choice.

requests_per_minute.description: How many requests the endpoint will accept per minute before it starts refusing with rate_limited.

burst.description: How many requests may arrive back to back before the per-minute rate applies, so a caller knows how much burst is tolerated.

max_turns.description: The most turns a single session will accept before it must be closed and a new one started.

session.title: session
session.description: Session policy. At endpoint level this is a default that each agent may override; at agent level it is that agent's own policy. A session is an envelope of identity and metadata, never conversation content, and the id format is deliberately absent because the server mints ids and a caller must treat them as opaque.

ttl_seconds.description: How long a session stays open without activity before it expires, in seconds. A caller should refresh before this elapses rather than discover the expiry when a turn fails.
